title: How a restaurant surcharge led the Port to recover six years of rent

beats.text: At Fisherman’s Wharf, a restaurant paid the Port a share of its sales.

visual.sub: One restaurant’s percentage rent depended on what counted as a sale

beats.text: The lease set that share at 6.75 percent.

visual.kicker: One restaurant’s percentage rent depended on what counted as a sale

beats.text: Cioppino’s left $581,102 in health surcharges out of reported sales.

visual.label: Customer health surcharges accounted for nearly all the underpayment

beats.text: The restaurant said it spent more on employee benefits than it collected from guests.

visual.kicker: Customer health surcharges accounted for nearly all the underpayment

beats.text: Two reporting errors left $39,534 in rent underpaid.

visual.label: Monthly sales adjustments added $310 in rent

beats.text: Receipts were understated in all 36 months. The audit cost $12,000.

visual.kicker: Every month exceeded a threshold found in other Port leases

beats.text: Other Port leases used a three percent threshold to pass audit costs to tenants.
This lease left that decision to the Port. It chose to absorb the cost.

visual.kicker: Every month exceeded a threshold found in other Port leases

beats.text: The Port checked earlier years too.

visual.kicker: The Port recovered rent for years outside the audit

beats.text: For 2008 through 2013, it reported recovering $76,767 in rent.

visual.label: The Port recovered rent for years outside the audit

beats.text: Every source is linked in the case file below.
